contents: A 38-year-old Caucasian woman with a history of two cesarean sections, the last one being in November 2015, presents with a painful, palpable, small, firm mass approximately 2 to 3 cm located on the lower abdominal wall at the cesarean section scar site. The mass shows no mobility to deeper anatomical planes. Her pain is cyclic, with symptoms starting three months after her last C-section. She has a known mild form of hereditary thrombophilia, but no other known lesions. An ultrasound reveals an irregular, heterogeneous, hypoechoic, oblong solid mass with ill-defined margins within the subcutaneous fat, infiltrating the abdominal muscle. What is the likely diagnosis for this mass?

A 46-year-old right-handed man presented with a one-year history of behavioral change, language impairment, and cognitive deficits. He became socially withdrawn, apathetic, and had poor self-care, with obsessive tendencies and a preference for routines. He experienced difficulty understanding word meanings and recognizing faces and familiar places, sometimes getting lost. On examination, his speech was noted to be fluent but empty, and he used stock phrases repeatedly. He was anomic with poor comprehension and showed surface dyslexia. Neuropsychometric testing revealed a verbal IQ of 73 and performance IQ of 125, with deficits in naming and verbal fluency. A strong family history of dementia was noted; his mother and most of her siblings developed "dementia" in their later years. MRI showed bilateral anterior temporal lobe atrophy more marked on the left, and less marked frontal lobe involvement. Based on these findings, what could be the possible diagnosis?

A 15-year-old female with no relevant past medical history presented with a 6-day history of left hip pain and limping. Physical examination showed reduced straight leg raise on the left side and reduced active and passive range of motion at the left hip with a block to internal and external rotation. The patient was afebrile, and laboratory investigations were unremarkable except for an elevated C-reactive protein of 13. A pelvic radiograph showed no abnormality, but MRI revealed a moderate left hip effusion of intermediate T1 signal, suggesting hemosiderin content, along with hypointense filling defects in the anterior recess of the joint. What could be the diagnosis?

A previously healthy 5-year-old boy had been receiving intravenous vancomycin for 26 days for osteomyelitis. He exhibited clinical and laboratory improvement but then suddenly developed a generalized erythematous maculopapular and pruritic rash on the face, trunk, back, and limbs, followed by a high-grade fever up to 40°C and weakness. Bilateral cervical and inguinal lymphadenopathy were noted, along with facial, neck, and scrotal edema. Laboratory findings revealed progressive leukocytosis and eosinophilia, minimal alterations in liver function tests, increased LDH levels, mildly elevated CRP, and altered coagulation tests with prolonged INR and elevated d-dimer. Renal function and electrolytes were normal. Virological and autoimmune tests were negative. A skin biopsy showed eosinophilic infiltration. What is the likely diagnosis?

A 12-year-old male presented with complaints of mobile teeth for the last 6 months. His deciduous teeth exfoliated at the age of 3, and by age 10, several permanent teeth had been extracted due to mobility. The remaining permanent teeth show varying degrees of flaring and mobility. Examination revealed severe gingival inflammation, thick plaque accumulation, and deep periodontal pockets. Bilateral hyperkeratotic plaques are present on the palms and soles. Radiographic examination indicates alveolar bone loss associated with the affected teeth, and third molar buds are present with normal crown development. What is the diagnosis for these clinical findings?

A 51-year-old South Asian man on maintenance hemodialysis presented with an acutely painful and swollen left thigh, along with breathlessness. He has a 20-year history of poorly controlled type 2 diabetes with nephropathy and retinopathy. Physical examination showed a temperature of 38.6 °C, pulse of 90 bpm, and blood pressure of 150/78 mmHg. He had bibasal chest crepitations and bilateral pedal edema. Laboratory tests revealed a C-reactive protein level of 147 mg/L and a white cell count of 8.7×10^9/L. Initial treatment with meropenem was provided for presumed sepsis due to cellulitis or an infective collection, following a Doppler ultrasound that excluded deep vein thrombosis and suggested superficial tissue edema. Blood cultures were negative. Subsequent MRI showed an abnormal signal from the anterior and medial thigh muscle compartments, indicative of an inflammatory or infective process. What could be the underlying diagnosis causing these symptoms?

A 69-year-old male presents with a progressive frontal paroxysmal headache, mild vomiting, diplopia, and visual disturbance for 1 month. He denies having fever. His visual acuity is 0.6 in the left eye and 0.9 in the right eye without visual field loss. He has a history of well-controlled hypertension and coronary heart disease, but no history of fungal infection or unusual infectious contact. Imaging reveals a mass in the sphenoid sinus and clival region with bone destruction. MRI shows hypointense T2-weighted signals in the lesions, and isointense T1-weighted signals with heterogeneous gadolinium-enhancement involving the sphenoid sinus, both cavernous sinuses, bilateral ethmoid sinuses, and maxillary sinus. What is the likely diagnosis?

A seven-year-old girl with a history of lymph node tuberculosis currently on anti-tuberculosis treatment presents with generalized tonic-clonic seizures, progressive intracranial hypertension characterized by treatment-resistant headaches, vomiting, fever, and alteration in general state. On examination, she is febrile (39°C), has lost 6kg over 5 months, and displays small cervical lymphadenopathies. Cerebral MRI reveals necrotic nodules in the left hemisphere with surrounding edema and meningeal granulations. Biological tests show an accelerated sedimentation rate, microcytic hypochromic anemia, neutrophilic leukocytosis, and a positive tuberculin skin test. The CSF analysis indicates hypoglycorrhachic lymphocytic meningitis. Based on these findings, what is the most likely diagnosis?

A previously healthy 10-year-old female patient presented with pain and swelling in her left elbow. Her medical history includes surgical intervention at age eight due to limited movement in the elbow. Excisional biopsy revealed subcutaneous tissue with widespread calcification. She was referred for recurring bilateral calcinosis in her elbows and right upper thigh. Her family history shows she is the offspring of a first-degree cousin marriage. Physical examination found warm, hard, and tender masses of 3 to 6 cm diameter in the left elbow, right elbow, and right upper thigh. Laboratory results showed marked hyperphosphatemia, normal serum creatinine, 25-hydroxyvitamin D, and parathormone levels, with an elevated TmP/GFR ratio. Radiographs showed radio-opaque masses around the elbows and right femur diaphysis. Dental and ophthalmological exams revealed no involvement. What is the likely diagnosis?

A 25-year-old woman presented with progressive difficulty in balance over three years, along with slurred speech and hand tremors over the last six months. She exhibits no visual disturbance, extremity weakness, or bladder/bowel issues. Physical examination shows dysarthria and intention tremor, but no cranial nerve abnormalities or motor/sensory deficits. Serum tests for autoimmune diseases and infections were negative. Imaging reveals irregular liver texture and bilateral hyperintensities on the basal ganglia and thalamus. Laboratory tests confirm low serum ceruloplasmin and high urinary copper excretion. Considering these symptoms and findings, what could be the diagnosis?

A 43-year-old right-hand-dominant male with a history of axial SpA and heavy smoking presents with bilateral digital ischaemia, worse on the right side. Six weeks prior, he developed blisters on his fingers. Despite vasodilator infusions and medical treatment, ischaemia progressed. Examination revealed a profoundly ischaemic right hand with fixed mottling, reduced motor function, and negative serological markers for vasculitis. An urgent CT angiogram showed bilateral cervical ribs, compression of the right subclavian artery in the abduction position, and occlusion of the right brachial artery due to thrombosis. What is the most likely diagnosis?

A 44-year-old woman with no significant medical history presents with 5 months of pelvic pain, vaginal discharge, intermittent fever, and significant weight loss of 30 kg. Physical examination reveals multiple abdominal masses. Imaging studies including tomography and MRI show collections in the peritoneal cavity with thickened walls and a complex, septate ovarian mass suggesting advanced neoplastic disease. Extension studies show no evidence of metastasis. Initial biopsy reveals lymphoplasmacytic inflammatory infiltrate, but no granulomas or malignancies. Despite negative cultures for aerobes, anaerobes, fungi, mycobacteria, and PCR for M. tuberculosis, histopathology reveals abscessed chronic inflammation with a mixed inflammatory infiltrate, abundant neutrophils, foamy histiocytes, and large filamentous radiated structures formed by gram-positive bacilli. What is the most likely diagnosis for this patient's condition?

A 54-year-old man with no relevant previous medical history presents with a progressive headache lasting seven months, episodic memory deficits, abnormal speech, disorientation, right hemiparesis, and unstable gait. On admission, he exhibits slight disorientation, right hemiparesis, anomia, and motor aphasia. Brain MRI reveals a mass in the left parietal lobe, periventricular white matter lesions, semioval center involvement, right temporal and ipsilateral occipital involvement, leptomeningeal enhancement, and bilateral bleeding areas predominantly in the left brain. MRI angiography shows multiple segmental areas of thinning at the middle cerebral artery suggestive of vasculitis, also present in the anterior cerebral artery. Laboratory tests return negative for carcinoembryonic antigen, syphilis serology, HIV, IgG and IgM anticardiolipin, antineutrophil cytoplasmic antibodies, antinuclear antibodies, and other specific autoimmune antibodies. What is the most likely diagnosis for this clinical presentation?

A 56-year-old Caucasian male has been admitted multiple times with recurrent abdominal pain described as intermittent cramping in the epigastrium, radiating to the left lower quadrant, accompanied by nausea, vomiting, and watery diarrhea. The pain worsens in the supine position and improves when sitting upright. The patient reports excessive thirst and frequent urination but denies fever, chills, dysuria, or hematuria. Persistent hypercalcemia and renal insufficiency are noted, with serum calcium levels at 13.3 and 13.5 mg/dL and acute renal insufficiency with BUN 44 mg/dL and creatinine levels of 2.1 mg/dL. Serum angiotensin-converting enzyme level is elevated at 98 units/L. 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D levels are elevated, while parathyroid hormone levels are appropriately suppressed. Despite normal chest X-ray findings, CT chest reveals subtle mediastinal adenopathy. What could be the underlying diagnosis for this clinical presentation?

A 30-year-old woman presented with a 3-week history of intermittent vaginal bleeding, hypertension, moderate pitting edema in both lower limbs, leukocytosis, severe anemia, thrombocytopenia, and high fever of 38.1 °C. Laboratory tests in our hospital revealed elevated CRP, hypoalbuminemia, abnormal renal function, and decreased complement levels. Imaging showed lymphadenopathy and hepatosplenomegaly, with increased FDG uptake in lymph nodes. Initial treatments, including hemodialysis and antibiotics, were ineffective, but glucocorticoid therapy led to improvement in CRP and APTT levels, though anemia and thrombocytopenia persisted. Lymph node biopsy revealed atrophic germinal centers and endothelial vessel proliferation, and further testing showed elevated IL-6 and VEGF levels. Based on the clinical picture and biopsy results, what is the most likely diagnosis?

A 7-year-old boy was referred to the endocrine clinic for short stature. He was born at full term without complications, with a birth weight of 3 kg, and has an unremarkable family history. During childhood, he received all vaccinations and had not been hospitalized. On examination, he appeared well without any abnormal facial features. He weighed 19 kg and was 101 cm in height, which placed him 3.6 standard deviations below the expected height for his age based on midparental predicted length. His vital organ sounds and abdominal examination were normal. Testicular volume was 3 ml each with Tanner stage 1 pubic hair distribution and penile size. Routine blood tests and urine and stool tests were mostly normal, except for mild anemia. A plain film of the left wrist indicated a bone age of a three-year-old, which was over 2 SD below chronological age. A growth hormone stimulation test revealed growth hormone deficiency. Further evaluation of other pituitary hormones showed central hypothyroidism and adrenal insufficiency. What could be the underlying diagnosis based on these findings?

A 14-year-old female patient presents with a chief complaint of teeth mobility and difficulty in mastication over a 2-year period due to loss of permanent teeth. Her past dental history includes early shedding of deciduous teeth and loss of many permanent teeth due to excessive mobility. She has a history of thickening of the skin on her palms and soles since childhood, with the rest of the family, including parents and a sibling, being unaffected. Intraoral examination reveals pathologically migrated teeth with various degrees of mobility and inflamed gingiva with deep periodontal pockets. A panoramic radiograph shows significant alveolar bone loss. Extraoral examination shows increased keratinization of the skin on her palms and plantar surfaces, with hyperhidrosis and malodor, but normal nails and hair. What could be the diagnosis?

A 58-year-old female patient presents with gradually worsening unsteady gait, numbness and tingling in hands and feet. She had a thyroidectomy operation 6 weeks ago with 60 minutes of general anesthesia involving nitrous oxide. Neurological examination shows slight weakness of distal muscles, bilaterally absent ankle reflexes, extensor plantar reflexes, and loss of position and vibration senses in all extremities. Romberg's sign is positive. Lab tests indicate increased mean corpuscular volume and low vitamin B12 levels, while folate and serum copper levels are normal. Brain MRI is unremarkable but cervical spinal cord MRI reveals high signal lesions in the posterior columns. What is the likely diagnosis?

An 18-year-old Japanese man presents with impaired consciousness and fluctuating ability to answer questions, alongside a sore throat and cough a week before admission. He exhibits a slight fever, normal pupils with a prompt light reflex, unrestricted eye movement, no gross muscle weakness, but decreased tendon reflexes in all extremities and absent plantar reflexes. Initial laboratory tests show elevated C-reactive protein and a white blood cell count with neutrophilia, though cerebrospinal fluid is clear with normal opening pressure and glucose levels, but a slight albuminocytologic dissociation is noted later. MRI scans reveal no brain abnormalities. Given these clinical findings, what is the likely diagnosis?

A 25-year-old primigravida at 23 weeks of gestation is presented with fetal intrauterine growth restriction (IUGR). The family history is unremarkable, and first-trimester screening for chromosomal aneuploidies was normal. Ultrasound reveals fetal measurements below the 5th centile, indicating severe symmetrical IUGR. Umbilical artery Doppler shows reverse end-diastolic flow, and pulsatility index is above the 95th centile. Uterine artery pulsatility indices are also increased bilaterally with notches. Amniotic fluid is reduced (AFI < 5). No fetal malformations are visible due to limited imaging. Given these findings, what is the potential underlying genetic condition?

A 19-year-old girl was admitted to the gynecology clinic with the complaint of primary amenorrhea. She appears phenotypically female and has normal external genitalia and breast development, but pubic and axillary hair are absent. There are bilateral palpable masses in the inguinal regions. Trans abdominal ultrasonography reveals these masses as immature testes, and a karyotype analysis shows a 46, XY chromosomal pattern. Routine blood tests are normal, but there is slightly elevated luteinizing hormone (LH). What is the most likely diagnosis?

A 21-month-old previously healthy boy presents with weakness of the lower extremities and lumbar pain following a mild upper respiratory tract infection. Initial evaluation with a hip ultrasound ruled out joint effusion, leading to a diagnosis of transient hip arthritis, for which he was treated with anti-inflammatory therapy. However, his symptoms worsened, resulting in hospitalization due to inability to walk and continued pain. Upon admission, spine radiography showed slight reduction in the thickness of the L5 vertebra. Subsequently, MRI revealed T1 post-enhancement increased signals at the L4-L5 annulus, the end-plates of L4 and L5, adjacent soft tissues, and the L5 pedicle's osteolytic area. Further tests showed an elevated erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR) and C-reactive protein (CRP) levels, normal white blood cell count, and negative results for tuberculosis. What is the likely diagnosis for this child's condition?

A 9-year-old female presents with a history of a low-intensity trauma followed by the development of a hard, slightly warm, non-painful swelling in the right latero-cervical/scapular region. This was followed by a new swelling lesion developing in the dorsal region, along with inguinal lymphadenopathy. On physical examination, the patient displays bilateral hallux valgus deformity, two frontal café-au-lait spots, and a lumbar angioma. An MRI of the soft tissue shows hyperintense signals in various muscle groups with postcontrast enhancement, while an X-ray of the foot reveals mild hallux valgus, triphalangism, and accessory distal epiphyseal nucleus. What could be the underlying diagnosis?

A 35-year-old Filipino female with advanced chronic kidney disease secondary to medullary cystic kidney disease presented with dyspnoea after four days of peritoneal dialysis training. She was otherwise well, afebrile, and her blood tests and ECG were unchanged. Clinical examination revealed a large right-sided pleural effusion, confirmed by chest radiograph. Diagnostic aspiration showed serous fluid with transudative characteristics, and a high pleural-fluid-serum-glucose ratio was noted. What is the likely diagnosis for her condition?

A 37-year-old man, employed as a warehouse keeper, presented with perioral chorea, dysphagia, dysarthria, vocalization, and involuntary upper limb movements over the past 5 months. His symptoms have progressively worsened and are further aggravated by involuntary self-mutilation behaviors, such as tongue and lip biting. He has a history of generalized tonic–clonic seizure at age 30, which has been in remission with sodium valproate. Neurological examination showed perioral chorea, reduced muscle tone, decreased tendon reflexes, and sporadic mouth ulcers along with frequent suck-mimicking activities. Laboratory tests indicated elevated serum creatine kinase, lactate dehydrogenase, and alpha hydroxybutyrate dehydrogenase, with creatine kinase levels reaching seven times the normal limit. A brain MRI revealed moderate dilation of the anterior horn of the lateral ventricles and mild atrophy of the caudate nucleus head. Blood smear tests revealed acanthocytes in 18% of the complete blood count. What is the most likely diagnosis for this patient?

A 67-year-old male patient with a history of hypertension, cardiac arrhythmia, acute hepatitis, and significant asbestos exposure, presented with right-sided pleural effusion. A CT scan showed pleural thickening, marked pleural effusion, and mediastinal lymphadenopathy, alongside a consolidative mass in the upper lobe with bronchovascular bundle and septal thickening, suggesting lung parenchymal involvement and lymphangitic spread. Biopsies of the pericardium and pleura were performed. What is the likely diagnosis?

A 58-year-old male presented with continuous lancinating pain in the right maxillary quadrant radiating to the temporal region, resulting in a headache. There is a history of COVID-19 infection a month ago, treated with steroid therapy, and a four-year history of diabetes. Extra-oral examination showed diffuse, tender swelling on the left side of the face, while intra-oral examination revealed mobility in all teeth of the first quadrant and inflamed palatal gingiva extending to the mid-palatine raphe. Cone beam computed tomography illustrated breach in the buccal and palatal cortical bone with scattered hypodense areas in the right anterior and posterior region, and bone destruction along the walls of the right and left maxillary sinuses. What is the possible diagnosis?

A 61-year-old woman of mixed Kuwaiti and Iraqi descent experienced progressive balance disturbance and fluctuating consciousness with a Glasgow Coma Scale ranging from 3 to 13/15. She had intermittent focal onset seizures, and abdominal pseudo-obstruction requiring flatus tube insertion on two occasions. Cerebrospinal fluid analysis revealed a moderate increase in lactate (4.5 mmol/L, reference range 1.1–2.4 mmol/L). Brain MRI three weeks after symptom onset showed multifocal areas of recent parenchymal insult with cortical and subcortical white matter signal abnormalities affecting different vascular territories. Past medical history included recurrent episodes of subacute neurological disturbance, diabetes, hearing loss, and a family history of diabetes and stroke. Given these symptoms and findings, what is the most likely diagnosis?

A 68-year-old female underwent an elective laparoscopic cholecystectomy and initially had an uneventful surgical and anaesthetic course. Her medical history included long-standing hypertension and previous breast carcinoma surgery. In the recovery ward, her blood pressure was elevated at 205/100 mmHg, partially resolving with opioid analgesia. The following day, she developed atrial fibrillation with a rate of 170 bpm, severe hypertension (BP 220/160 mmHg), pulmonary oedema, and lactic acidosis. She became progressively hypotensive and obtunded, requiring intubation and mechanical ventilation. Despite unremarkable initial CT scans of brain, chest, and abdomen, further investigation showed severe systolic impairment on echocardiogram and normal coronary arteries on angiography. A nodule was later identified on the right adrenal gland. With elevated urinary catecholamines and plasma metanephrines, what could be the underlying cause of her hypertensive crisis and subsequent cardiogenic shock?

A 7-year-old boy presents with a 1-year history of excruciating unilateral headache located in the right orbito-frontal region. The headaches last from 5 to 30 minutes and occur 1–3 times per day at both day and night. The pain is accompanied by ipsilateral autonomic symptoms, such as conjunctival injection, eyelid edema, and rhinorrhea, as well as migraine-like features like vomiting and photophobia. Neurological examinations and imaging tests, including CT, MRI, and EEG, are normal. The headaches have not responded to various non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs or to prophylactic treatment with amitriptyline, but showed significant improvement with indomethacin. What is the most likely diagnosis for this child's condition?

A 71-year-old woman presented with dysarthria and impaired ambulation, and had a clinical history of progressive left hemibody myoclonus, facial nerve dysfunction, and mild diffuse hypertonia. She had been progressively worsening in clinical and behavioral symptoms, becoming noncompliant, soporous, hostile, and disoriented. Laboratory tests revealed hypogammaglobulinemia and severe lymphocytopenia. An EEG was normal, but hyperactive deep tendon reflexes were observed. MRI showed cortical-subcortical abnormal hyperintensity areas on FLAIR images in both cerebral hemispheres, with SWI imaging revealing several punctate hypointensities indicating cortical hemosiderin deposits. Gadolinium contrast revealed gyral enhancement of these lesions on T1-weighted images. What is the most likely diagnosis?

A 68-year-old male presents with recurrent cough, expectoration, and progressive dyspnea for over 30 years. Previously misdiagnosed with chronic bronchitis, bronchiectasis, and endobronchial tuberculosis, he received multiple antibiotic treatments without improvement. Examination reveals diminished breath sounds, slight bibasilar wheezing rales, and crackles. Routine blood tests are normal, and sputum samples negative for bacteria, acid-fast bacilli, and fungi. Chest CT shows extensive tracheal and bronchial wall thickening with luminal narrowing. Bronchoscopy reveals swelling and hypertrophy of tracheal and bronchial mucosa. A biopsy indicates chronic inflammation and amyloid deposition with positive Congo red stain. What is the likely diagnosis?

An eight-year-old girl presented with right ear hearing loss. She passed hearing screening at birth, but noticed difficulty in daily communication starting at approximately six years of age. A pure tone audiometry test showed profound hearing loss in the right ear while her left ear had normal hearing. Auditory brainstem response examination revealed poorly identified waves in the right ear, and distortion product otoacoustic emissions were absent in the right ear, indicating severe unilateral sensorineural hearing loss. Temporal bone CT and MRI showed no structural abnormalities. Quantitative polymerase chain reaction for CMV DNA was negative in stored dried umbilical cord. Serum analysis showed elevated anti-CMV IgG antibody levels, undetectable anti-CMV IgM and anti-mumps IgM antibody levels, and significantly elevated anti-Sjögren's syndrome-A antibody levels. The Saxon test indicated decreased saliva production, and salivary gland biopsy showed numerous plasma and lymphocyte infiltrations. What is the most likely diagnosis?

A 25-year-old male with no prior co-morbidities presented to the ED in August 2020 with a high-grade, intermittent fever for four days, associated with chills, vomiting, and loose stools. He also reported a sudden onset, severe throbbing headache in the bilateral frontal region with photophobia and phonophobia, and exhibited neck stiffness on examination. The patient had no blurring of vision, weakness, numbness, altered mentation, seizures, or loss of consciousness. He was vitally stable and alert upon arrival at the ED. CSF analysis showed an elevated total leukocyte count with 84% lymphocytes, and an MRI brain was unremarkable. What could be the likely diagnosis for this patient's symptoms?

A 38-year-old male presents with excruciating posterior left sided neck pain for four days, dysphagia, and neck stiffness. Initial concerns include an abscess of the deep spaces of the neck. A CT scan reveals a prevertebral retropharyngeal low attenuation collection spanning from C1 to C5, along with dystrophic calcifications anterior to C1 and C2, but no enhancement of the fluid collection, neck adenopathy, or bone destruction, ruling out retropharyngeal abscess. An MRI confirms the presence of retropharyngeal effusion. The patient's symptoms improve significantly with Ketorolac and Acetaminophen after hospitalization. What is the likely diagnosis?

A 47-year-old white woman presented to an outside hospital with subacute and progressive dizziness, diplopia, dysarthria, and bilateral ptosis, which started 8 hours prior to admission. Cranial computed tomography (CT) and magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) revealed normal results. A cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) analysis was normal. Her neurological symptoms worsened rapidly, including complete bilateral ptosis with inability to open her eyes, descending quadriparesis, and paralysis of her respiratory musculature. Approximately 24 hours following admission, she required intubation and mechanical ventilation. Her husband presented with similar signs and symptoms a day later. The patient recalled having eaten home-canned beans of unknown age 2 days prior to the admission. What could be the diagnosis for this sudden onset of severe neurological symptoms?

A 76-year-old female presented with a fever up to 38.2°C, somnolence, cough, nausea, anomic aphasia, disorientation, and a lack of neck stiffness. Her vital signs included a BP of 150/80 mmHg, temperature of 37.8°C, SpO2 of 94%, and pulse rate of 77 bpm. Blood tests showed WBC 5150, 84% neutrophils, and CRP 0.03 mg/dl. Lumbar puncture revealed CSF with 75 cells/mm3, predominantly lymphocytes (94%), glucose of 77 mg/dl, and total protein of 53.8 mg/dl. Brain MRI displayed hyperintensity in the left temporal lobe and insula. What is the most likely diagnosis for this patient?

A twelve-year-old boy presents with weight loss, hot flushes, palpitations, and diaphoresis for the past month. His blood pressure is elevated at 140/100 mmHg, and his heart rate is 115 beats per minute. Laboratory tests reveal an increased 24-hour urinary vanillylmandelic acid concentration of 115 mg/day. Abdominal ultrasound and MRI show solid masses in both adrenal glands. What is the most likely diagnosis?

A 4-year and 6-month-old boy has been experiencing recurrent lung infections and hematuria for over two years. Physical examination shows visible tonsils, cervical, axillary, and inguinal lymphadenectasis, dry rales in both lungs, and no murmurs in the heart. Abdominal examination reveals softness with enlarged liver and spleen. No signs are noted in the nervous system examination. Laboratory findings include increased urine red blood cells, high titers of anti-neutrophil cytoplasmic antibody (ANCA) for PR3, and EB and CMV IgM detection. Imaging studies show pulmonary nodules, bronchiectasis, sinusitis, and patchy infiltration in the lung, along with bilateral maxillary and ethmoid sinusitis. Biopsies indicate reactive lymph node hyperplasia, slight glomerular lesions from renal biopsy, lymphocyte infiltration around bronchioles with collagen fiber hyperplasia in lung biopsy, and granulocyte hyperplasia in bone marrow. Initial treatment with oral prednisone and cyclophosphamide improved hematuria but recurrent lung infections persisted. Genetic testing reveals a mutation E1021K (c.3061 G >A) in the PIK3CD gene. What is the most likely diagnosis for this boy?

A 56-year-old Japanese man was referred to our hospital for investigation of tarry stool. He had been consuming lansoprazole, irsogladine, metoprolol, flutoprazepam, and ethyl loflazepate for gastritis, hypertension, and anxiety disorder, with no history of dyslipidemia or diabetes mellitus. Physical examination showed no abnormalities in his abdomen and no xanthomas on his skin, while laboratory findings revealed normal levels of cholesterol, triglyceride, and plasma glucose. Esophagogastroduodenoscopy indicated erosive and atrophic gastritis. During colonoscopy, multiple yellowish spots measuring approximately 3 to 5 mm were observed in the rectum, in addition to hemorrhoids. Magnifying observation with narrow-band imaging indicated intact pits of the rectal mucosa, and indigo-carmine spraying highlighted the whitish to yellowish color of the lesions. What is the likely diagnosis based on these colonoscopy findings?

A 3-month-old male infant shows signs of neurodevelopmental delay and movement disorders after normal birth metrics. He has feeding problems, regurgitations, dystonic postures, and spontaneous Moro reflex. His neurologic examination reveals decreased tone of neck muscles, spasticity of extremities, hyperreflexia, persistent primitive reflexes, and jerky movements. Psychomotor delay is noted with a developmental quotient of 35. Transfontanelle sonography shows slightly dilated lateral ventricles and a large cyst-like cisterna magna suggesting cerebellar hypoplasia. His older sister has been diagnosed with dyskinetic cerebral palsy, presenting similar neurodevelopmental issues and microcephaly. What is the likely diagnosis?

A 31-year-old white Hispanic woman presented with a 5-month history of epigastric pain. She did not present with any other symptoms. An abdominal ultrasound revealed a 2 cm, single nodule in the uncinate process of her pancreas. Endoscopic ultrasound (EUS) showed a well-defined hypoechoic solid lesion with regular, clear, and precise margins and alternating cystic areas measuring 1.7 × 1.4 cm, located in the uncinate process of her pancreas. The lesion had no communication with her main pancreatic duct. What is the most likely diagnosis for this pancreatic lesion?

A 12-year-old boy was admitted with high-grade fever, weakness, and a generalized erythematous eruption. He has a history of epilepsy and started valproic acid (VPA) treatment three weeks prior to admission. On examination, he is alert, with a fever of 39°C, pulse rate of 88 bpm, respiration rate of 18 breaths/min, and blood pressure of 110/75 mmHg. Skin examination shows a generalized maculopapular rash that partly confluent to plaques on the body, face, and back. He has facial edema and hepatomegaly but no lymphadenopathy. Laboratory tests reveal hemoglobin at 12.2 g/dL, leukocyte count of 3.07 × 10^3/mm3 with 20% neutrophils, 64% lymphocytes (including 7% atypical lymphocytes), and 16% eosinophils. Liver enzymes—AST, ALT, ALP, and GGT—are elevated, and CRP is 30.2 mg/dL. ESR is 50 mm/h. Blood and throat cultures are negative. Virology tests for hepatitis A, B, C, Epstein-Barr virus, parvovirus B-19, human herpesvirus type 6, and cytomegalovirus are negative, as are antistreptolysin O, anti-double-stranded DNA, and ANA profiles. LDH is elevated at 936 U/L, and VPA level is 97.5 μg/mL. Ultrasonography shows hepatosplenomegaly. Based on these findings, what could be the diagnosis?

A 64-year-old male presented with worsening abdominal pain, constipation, nausea, and vomiting for the last 3 days. He denied chest pain, palpitations, dizziness, shortness of breath, or loss of consciousness. He has been passing hard stool and a small amount of gas. His past medical history includes diabetes mellitus, hypertension, chronic kidney disease, as well as multiple abdominal surgeries. On examination, he was lethargic and dehydrated with a distended and tender abdomen; bowel sounds were high pitched. Erect abdominal X-ray showed scattered air-fluid levels, and CT confirmed the diagnosis. Surprisingly, his ECG showed sinus tachycardia with inferolateral ST elevation, while cardiac biomarkers and echocardiography results did not indicate an acute coronary event. What could be the diagnosis for this presentation?

An 8-year-old boy presented with complaints of tooth decay on his right lower back tooth. Examination revealed brachycephaly, frontal bossing, sloping shoulders, and a narrow palate with high vault. Dental examination showed several retained deciduous teeth with missing second premolars in both arches, along with anterior and posterior crossbites. A chest radiograph indicated total absence of clavicles and a bell-shaped thorax, while a skull radiograph showed widening of sutures and wormian bones. There is an abnormal increased vertical growth pattern of the mandible. Given these findings, what could be the underlying diagnosis?

A 69-year-old Japanese man presents with anorexia and significant weight loss. He has a past medical history of hypertension, dyslipidemia, and glaucoma. He underwent endoscopic resection for early-stage colon cancer after presenting with lower abdominal pain. Despite persistent abdominal symptoms, imaging showed only mildly enlarged supraclavicular and para-aortic lymph nodes. Laboratory findings revealed proteinuria (3+) of 1.4 g/day, microhematuria, low complement levels, elevated eosinophil count, and significantly elevated serum IgG and IgG4 levels. A renal biopsy showed focal interstitial fibrosis with infiltration by mononuclear cells, eosinophils, and numerous IgG4-positive plasma cells, alongside global thickening of the glomerular basement membrane with subepithelial deposits but no glomerular sclerosis or crescent formation. Given these findings, what is the likely diagnosis?

A 7-year-old male presented with a painless right facial mass for one year. On examination, he had a 3 cm right parotid mass that was firm, nonpulsatile, and nontender with no overlying skin changes, and his facial nerve was intact. He had no constitutional symptoms. Fine needle aspiration of the mass demonstrated diffusely small lymphocytes admixed with occasional macrophages, suggestive of a reactive lymph node. An MRI contrast study revealed a well-circumscribed homogenously T1 isointense and T2 hyperintense mass replacing nearly the entire right parotid gland and involving the deep lobe of the gland, measuring 3.0 × 3.1 × 3.6 cm. What is the most likely diagnosis for this parotid mass?

A 30-month-old boy was admitted to the pediatric intensive care unit with heart failure and respiratory distress. He had macropenis and excessive skin darkness. His height was 99 cm and blood pressure at the presentation was 143/98 mmHg. Imaging studies showed cardiomegaly and severe dilated cardiomyopathy. What is the likely diagnosis?

A 44-year-old woman was referred with a painless swelling in the left posterior region of the mandible that she had experienced for 2 years. The molar teeth in this area had been extracted. Radiological examination showed a large, well-defined, multilocular radiolucent lesion with scalloped borders extending from the first molar area into the ascending ramus, which perforated the cortex. Extraoral examination revealed no palpable lymph nodes in the neck. An incisional biopsy revealed microscopic islands of epidermoid, mucous, and intermediate cells with cystic areas in a fibrous stroma. What is the most likely diagnosis for this mandibular lesion?

A 12-year-old girl presents with a history of paleness, epigastric pain, and menorrhagia, along with microcytic hypochromic anemia (Hb = 10.6 g/dL; MCV = 64 fL; MCH = 19.4 pg; MCHC = 302 g/L; iron = 2.7 μmol/L; ferritin = 6 μg/L) that is unresponsive to oral iron treatment. A positive fecal occult blood test and elevated fecal calprotectin (705 μg/g) were noted, prompting upper and lower endoscopies. Helicobacter pylori tests were contradictory: fecal antigen was positive, requiring eradication therapy, but Giemsa-stained and immunohistochemical tests were negative. Follow-up endoscopy showed persistent gastritis. What is the likely diagnosis for this patient?

A 44-year-old Japanese male presented to the emergency department after a temporary loss of consciousness. He has experienced fatigue for 3 years and has been prone to falling in the past 2 months. Recently, he had a fever, cough, and phlegm for several days prior to admission and fell down the stairs feeling drowsy. He is thin, with a height of 174 cm and a weight of 52 kg. Chest computed tomography showed severe infiltration in the upper posterior fields of both lungs and food debris in the esophagus, leading to a diagnosis of aspiration pneumonia. His past medical history includes diabetes mellitus managed by a local doctor, and he has a family history of a father who died of dilated cardiomyopathy and a mother who is healthy. He also has a history of recurrent ileus. Upon neurological examination, he exhibited forehead balding, a hatchet face with bilateral ptosis, nasal speech, mild muscle weakness in all four extremities, handgrip myotonia, and diffuse muscle atrophy. Electromyography showed frequent myotonic discharges. What could be the underlying diagnosis?

A 13-year-old female has a long history of recurrent dull and aching pain in the right iliac fossa, unresponsive to analgesia and antibiotics. She reports no anorexia, weight loss, fever, lethargy, altered bowel habits, or urinary symptoms. Clinical examination shows she appears well with a soft abdomen, tender upon deep palpation in the right iliac fossa. Full blood count and urinalysis are normal. An ultrasound suggests appendicitis. During surgery, there is free fluid in the peritoneal cavity, a non-inflamed appendix with a yellowish tinge, and terminal ileal lymphadenopathy. What is the diagnosis?

A 26-year-old male presents with weakness, fever, generalized tonic clonic seizures along with urinary incontinence for a month. The seizures are associated with transient loss of consciousness and frothing from the mouth, which have occurred for the last 3 days. On examination, deep tendon reflexes are absent, plantar response is flexor, and facial muscle weakness is noted, though other cranial nerves are normal. Vital signs show a respiratory rate of 14/min, heart rate of 88/min, and blood pressure of 138/98 mmHg. After 18 days, he aspirates following a seizure episode leading to intubation and mechanical ventilation. Investigations are within normal limits except for a positive urine porphobilinogen. Given the clinical presentation and laboratory findings, what is the likely diagnosis?

A 55-year-old man presented with a history of taste disorder, specifically a loss of taste for sweet, sour, bitter, and salty flavors, while his sense of smell remained intact. Initial evaluations at the Otolaryngology and Stomatology Departments, as well as cranial magnetic resonance imaging, showed no significant abnormalities. After experiencing dysgeusia for six months, the patient developed blepharoptosis, which was mild in the morning and worsened by evening, particularly after fatigue. A positive neostigmine test and findings from SFEMG and RNS suggest a neurological cause. His AChR-Ab levels were elevated, while MuSK-Ab was negative. What is the most likely diagnosis?

A 42-year-old man presented for evaluation of a left buttock mass found incidentally at a general check-up. On physical examination, the mass was nontender, deep-seated, and elastic, with no local lymphadenopathy or associated discomfort. MRI revealed a well-circumscribed, slightly heterogeneous mass 12 cm in diameter between the gluteus medius and maximus muscles. The tumor signal was considerably higher than skeletal muscle but lower than subcutaneous fat on both T1- and T2-weighted images. Fat-suppressed T1-weighted images showed a mixture of low and intermediate signals. The mass demonstrated diffuse contrast enhancement following Gd-DTPA administration. FDG-PET/CT revealed increased FDG uptake with an SUVmax of 4.1. No other abnormal FDG uptake was found. What is the most likely diagnosis for this left buttock mass?

A 35-year-old woman presents with gradual onset, slowly progressive polyarthritis affecting the small and large joints of the hands in a rheumatoid distribution, along with nodules over her lower legs. She reports early morning stiffness that improves with activity. Initially, joint involvement began with the wrist, followed by transient knee and ankle arthritis. The nodules on her shins resolve after a few days, leaving hyperpigmented macules, and are accompanied by a feverish feeling. Laboratory tests show a normal haemogram, ESR of 29 mm/1st hour, and negative RF, CRP, and anti-CCP. ANA is positive. Examination reveals few lesions resembling erythema nodosum and synovitis of wrists, ankles, and small joints of the hand. Skin biopsy shows hyperkeratosis, acanthosis, perivascular infiltrate with neutrophils, lymphocytes, epithelioid cells, and foamy histiocytes. Fite staining reveals fragmented acid-fast bacilli with a bacteriological index of 3+ AFB from the slit skin smears. Given these findings, what is the most likely diagnosis?

A Japanese boy aged 5 years and 8 months was referred for malformation of the anterior primary and permanent teeth. His medical history was unremarkable, and no dental or maxillofacial abnormalities were reported in his family. Examination revealed an edentulous area in the left maxilla where primary central incisor, lateral incisor, and canine were missing. Previously extracted due to severe apical periodontitis. The primary maxillary left second molar was yellowish and had an irregular surface. Radiographs showed malformed and hypocalcified permanent maxillary teeth with unusual morphology, small size, and immature root formation. Dental follicles of affected teeth were enlarged. He exhibited a diminished tendency to erupt, and radiographs showed irregular expansion of dental follicles of affected teeth. What is the likely diagnosis for this dental condition?

An 8-year-old boy was incidentally found to have a splenic mass on abdominal ultrasonography during a routine check and was admitted for further investigation. He has no significant medical history, and physical examination and lab tests including blood routine, serum chemistry, and tumor biomarkers are unremarkable. Imaging studies reveal an isoechoic oval-shaped mass with smooth borders in the spleen, measuring 5.2 cm × 4.2 cm × 3.4 cm, with increased internal blood flow observed on Doppler ultrasound. A non-enhanced CT shows a slightly lower-density mass with poorly-defined margins, while a contrast-enhanced CT shows mild heterogeneous enhancement. MRI findings include a hypointense mass on T1WI and slightly hyperintense on T2WI, with moderate gadolinium enhancement. Differential diagnosis includes hemangiomas, angiosarcomas, primary splenic lymphoma, and inflammatory lesions. Given these findings, what is the likely diagnosis for this splenic mass?

An 11-year-old male presented with fever, sore throat, and ear pain lasting a week, initially diagnosed as acute otitis media and treated with oral antibiotics. One week later, he was unable to fully close his right eye and showed absent right nasolabial groove on neurological examination, leading to a diagnosis of Bell's palsy. He started oral methylprednisolone treatment (1 mg/kg/day). On the second day of treatment, painful blisters developed in his right ear, and he exhibited Grade 4 House-Brackmann facial paralysis. Laboratory tests, including complete blood count and erythrocyte sedimentation rate, were normal. Tympanometry was bilateral type A, and audiography showed pure-tone thresholds of 6 dB in the right ear and 5 dB in the left ear. What could be the diagnosis for this condition given the new symptoms?

A 10-year-old boy with acute lymphoblastic leukemia, receiving induction chemotherapy including intravenous L-asparaginase, presented with a headache that initially showed no focal lesions on plain CT. Two days later, his symptoms worsened with vomiting, seizures, and loss of consciousness. Noncontrast CT revealed bilateral hemorrhagic infarcts in the high parietal regions with a mass effect. Contrast-enhanced CT showed hypodense attenuation of the superior sagittal sinus with peripheral enhancement, known as the empty delta sign. Blood tests revealed significant coagulogram abnormalities, including antithrombin deficiency. What is the likely diagnosis given this clinical presentation?

A 57-year-old woman presented with sudden abdominal pain and fever. Her vital signs showed a blood pressure of 120/76 mmHg, heart rate of 102 beats/min, and body temperature of 38.2 °C. Tenderness was noted in the epigastrium and hypochondriac region without muscular defense or rebound tenderness. Laboratory tests indicated elevated hepato-biliary enzymes (T-bil: 2.7 mg/dL; GOT: 299 U/L; GPT: 535 U/L; ALP: 2459 U/L; γ-GTP: 2054 U/L) and mildly increased CA 19-9 levels (99.0 U/mL). HBsAg and HCVAb were negative, and there was no history of excessive alcohol consumption. Contrast CT revealed a multi-locular cystic lesion in the left hepatic lobe with internal septal formation. MRI showed low signal intensities on T1-weighted images and high on T2-weighted images inside the cystic lesion. ERCP revealed an oval-shaped filling defect in the common bile duct, with no malignancy in bile cytology. EUS showed the tumor occupying the common bile duct with many septal formations. What could be the underlying diagnosis?

A 63-year-old male presented with a 14-day history of pruritic erythematous papules over his entire body, accompanied by jaundice. Despite using a topical corticosteroid and an antihistamine for 10 days, his symptoms worsened, with eye and oral mucosal involvement. He began treatment with anti-hypertensive drugs 5 months ago and started allopurinol 3 weeks ago for gout. He exhibited a high fever (>38.0℃) during physical examination. Laboratory tests indicated elevated levels of aspartate aminotransferase (AST; 161 U/L), alanine aminotransferase (ALT; 390 U/L), total bilirubin (10.9 mg/dL), and eosinophils (2,432/mm2). The histopathological findings were compatible with erythema multiforme. What is the most likely diagnosis for this patient's condition?

A 66-year-old male patient presents with localized dermatosis from the right pelvis to the foot, including the central part and metatarsal region of the right foot. Examination reveals a tumorous lesion with fibrotic characteristics and several sinuses exuding purulent material. The patient experiences pain upon palpation and walking. The patient is a farmer from Tapachula, Chiapas, and reports multiple injuries over 18 years. Radiography shows slight osteolytic activity in the metatarsal bones. Direct examination of fistula exudate reveals large dark grains of filamentous consistency, and Sabouraud-dextrose agar culture shows a dark filamentous colony with brown-ocher pigment, along with multiple brown hyphae and clamydoconidia. A biopsy stained with haematoxylin and eosin reveals hyperkeratosis, irregular acanthosis, pseudoepitheliomatous hyperplasia, and a suppurative granulomatous process with lympho-histiocytic infiltrate forming microabscesses with dark hyphae grains. The patient has previously received treatments including sulphamethoxazole-trimethoprim, ketoconazole, and various topical treatments. Given these findings, what is the likely diagnosis?

A 33-year-old primigravida was referred to a tertiary center for fetal congenital heart disease at 21 weeks of gestation. The fetus had no suspected chromosomal abnormalities after amniocentesis. Fetal ultrasonography revealed tetralogy of Fallot, a single umbilical artery, and clinodactyly. At 30 weeks, ultrasound showed a possible shorter perineal body than expected for a normal female fetus. What condition might this indicate that requires diagnosis after birth?

A 28-year-old male presents with generalized bone aches, intermittent fever, and weight loss. Laboratory investigations reveal anemia, renal impairment, elevated uric acid, hypercalcemia, and normal white blood cell count without peripheral blasts. Bone marrow aspiration shows 95% blast cells. Whole body CT reveals multiple osteolytic lesions affecting the spine and various bones. Given these findings, what is the likely diagnosis?

A 12-year-old girl has a six-week history of recurrent pain and swelling of the right mandible that has progressively worsened. Initially treated with antibiotics for three weeks and needle aspiration at a local dental clinic under the assumption of infection, she now presents with prominent right facial swelling, erythema, tenderness at the angle and inferior border of the mandible, and newly developed cutaneous fistula. Regional lymphadenopathy is noted, but sensation in the lower lip and chin area remains intact. Intra-oral examination shows no caries lesions or periodontal pathology, with a maximal inter-incisal opening of 15 mm due to pain. Panoramic radiograph indicates overall sclerosis on the right mandible with a lytic lesion on the right mandibular third molar and a prominent proliferative periosteal reaction on the right mandible's angle, body, and sigmoid notch area. CT scan reveals widening of the follicular space of the right mandibular third molar, cortical perforation, and pus formation. Given these findings, what is the most likely diagnosis?

A 1-year-old male presented with a 2-week history of limping, fever, and difficulty moving the left leg. Physical examination showed no gross deformity, swelling, or skin lesions. Laboratory tests indicated leucocytosis, but other values were within normal limits. X-rays revealed a radiolucent lesion at the left proximal tibial meta-diaphysis with a periosteal reaction. What is the most likely diagnosis for this presentation?

A 15-year-old female with a history of anxiety, depression, and ADHD presents with 4 days of nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, and mild intermittent dry cough. She has been vaping nicotine pods and THC-containing products using open and closed system devices, but ceased vaping a week prior to symptom onset. Her examination reveals a heart rate of 116, respiratory rate of 34, oxygen saturation of 78%, and temperature of 100.5°F. Imaging studies show bilateral interstitial reticular opacities with trace bilateral pleural effusions on chest X-ray, and dependent lung consolidation with intralobular septal thickening on chest CT. CRP levels are highly elevated, and she is subsequently admitted to the PICU due to deteriorating respiratory status. She is treated empirically with IV antibiotics and later with IV methylprednisolone, with no infectious cause identified from extensive workup. Postdischarge spirometry is nonobstructive but shows mildly reduced diffusing capacity of the lungs for carbon monoxide (DLCO). What is the most likely diagnosis?

A 52-year-old woman presented with persistent orthostatic headaches. She underwent an MRI that demonstrated deformation and severe sagging of the midbrain with bilateral subdural hematomas. On the second hospital day, her GCS score acutely deteriorated to 8 (E2V1M5), and she developed bilateral miosis with bradycardia. After being placed in the Trendelenburg position, her GCS score improved back to 15 within 1 day. What is the likely diagnosis?

A 20-year-old right-handed African-American woman with a history of hypothyroidism and factor V Leiden homozygous presents with an insidious onset of right eye pain with movement, followed by blurred vision in the right eye after nine days. She denies any diplopia, headaches, or symptoms suggestive of viral infection. Ophthalmologist evaluation suggests acute right retrobulbar optic neuritis. Neurological and physical examinations are unremarkable, and MRI of the brain shows right optic nerve enhancement at the orbital apex. CSF studies reveal positive NMO/aquaporin-4 (AQP4) and a high serum NMO/AQP4-IgG titre. MRI of the thoracic spine shows small foci of increased T2 signal. What is the most likely diagnosis?

A 50-year-old male, working as forest security personnel, presented with generalized pruritic rashes persisting for 1 year, initially starting over the lower abdomen and later becoming widespread. Despite using multiple topical and oral steroids, his condition persisted. In the past month, he experienced fever, breathlessness, and chest pain. On skin examination, there were symmetrically distributed multiple confluent erythematous scaly plaques over the trunk and extremities, with some areas having well-defined margins. Additionally, he had multiple pearly white umbilicated papules on the forehead and bi-temporal areas. Oral examination revealed whitish plaques on the tongue that bled upon rubbing, and there was whitish discoloration with roughening at the proximal part of the right thumbnail. He was also diagnosed with exfoliative dermatitis, proximal subungual onychomycosis, extragenital molluscum contagiosum, chronic oral pseudomembranous candidiasis, sepsis, and bilateral tubercular pleural effusion, with choroid tubercles suggestive of intraocular tuberculosis. Potassium hydroxide (KOH) mount from skin scrapings and nail clippings showed multiple septate hyphae, confirming dermatophytic infection. Considering these symptoms and his history of high-risk sexual behavior, what is the likely underlying condition?

A 32-year-old Nigerian woman presents with a 1-month history of bilateral blurring of vision, red eyes, persistent headache, and tinnitus. She is 16 weeks pregnant. General examination shows significant alopecia and skin depigmentation on the forehead. Ophthalmic examination reveals visual acuity of counting fingers at 1 meter in both eyes, poliosis in the right eye, conjunctival congestion, and multiple medium-sized keratic precipitates on the corneal endothelium. Anterior chamber examination shows significant cells and flare, with both pupils showing posterior synechiae. The posterior segment examination reveals vitreous cells, bilateral exudative retinal detachment, and disc edema. Intraocular pressures are normal. Systemic examinations, including full blood count, retroviral screenings, and chest radiograph, return normal. Given these findings, what is the likely diagnosis?

A 12-year-old girl presented with a 2-week history of worsening epigastric pain, vomiting, and fever. Previously treated for gastroenteritis, her symptoms persisted, leading to her referral for further management. On examination, she appeared pale with dry mucous membranes, and had bradycardia (heart rate 68/min) and hypotension (blood pressure 90/60 mm Hg) with an increased respiratory rate (24/min). She exhibited muscle weakness in both lower limbs (power 4/5) and genu valgum, without bony pain or palpable neck lumps. Laboratory tests revealed hypercalcemia with hyperparathyroidism. An ultrasound showed a well-defined oval hypoechoic mass in the posteroinferior aspect of the left lobe of the thyroid gland. Radionuclide parathyroid scintigraphy identified an adenoma in the left inferior parathyroid gland. What could be the underlying diagnosis for this presentation?

A 44-year-old woman has experienced recurrent right mandibular pain for 6 years. Despite extensive diagnostic workup and two local excisions of the right mandible lesion, her pain persists. Eighteen months after her second mandible resection, she experiences left femur pain. Laboratory workup including ESR, CRP, and CBC is normal. X-Rays reveal an osteosclerotic lesion with cortical thickening and periosteal new bone formation in the left femur. A Technetium99 scan shows multiple locations of active uptake, including the right mandible, anterior chest wall, left pubic bone, and left femur. Biopsies are negative for malignancy or infection. What is the likely diagnosis?

A 71-year-old woman with a history of depression and hypertension underwent electroconvulsive therapy (ECT). Her medications included quetiapine, nortriptyline, metoprolol, amlodipine, and ativan. Following the ECT procedure, she experienced onset of chest pain. An ECG showed T wave flattening in AVL and poor precordial R wave progression. A troponin level was elevated, and cardiac catheterization showed non-obstructive coronary artery disease. Echocardiography revealed left ventricular dysfunction with an ejection fraction of 20% and a large apical aneurysm, which improved significantly upon follow-up. What is the likely diagnosis for this patient's condition post-ECT?

A 25-day-old male neonate was transferred to an emergency unit due to lethargy and general cyanosis. He was formula-fed from birth and started showing symptoms 7 days ago, including vomiting several times a day, mucous and loose stools, and mild fever. He developed weak sucking power and appeared malnourished, showing sepsis-like symptoms such as facial cyanosis and abdominal distention. Laboratory tests showed leukocytosis, thrombocytosis, hypoalbuminemia, metabolic acidosis, and methemoglobinemia. Imaging revealed pneumatosis intestinalis, subtotal villous atrophy, and portal venous gas. Blood, urine, and stool cultures were negative, and tests for milk allergy, amino acid analysis, immunoglobulins, and T cell subsets were normal. No vomiting or other adverse symptoms were seen after being fed extensively hydrolyzed formula. After reintroducing cow's milk, projectile vomiting and lethargy with pallor occurred, followed by improvement after fluid therapy. What is the diagnosis for this neonate's condition?

A 61-year-old man has been experiencing progressive blurring of his vision and visual field defects for the past 3 weeks, without any systemic problems or major medical history. Upon examination, he presented with left homonymous hemianopia, slight cortical cataracts, and normal optical coherence tomography. Initial brain imaging was normal, but his condition worsened, showing further decrease in visual acuity and worsening visual field defects, accompanied by dysarthria and gait disorder. Electroencephalography showed periodic sharp wave complexes, and cerebrospinal fluid analysis revealed high levels of 14-3-3 and total tau proteins, along with prion seeding activity. Diffusion-weighted MRI indicated high signal intensity in the cortex and occipital lobes. Considering these findings, what could be the underlying diagnosis for his symptoms?

An 82-year-old man presented with a chief complaint of an abdominal mass and associated abdominal discomfort, which he first noticed 4 years prior. A CT scan revealed a lipomatous retroperitoneal tumor that had been growing. Physical examination showed a large palpable abdominal mass, but no other specific abnormalities. An abdominal CT scan confirmed a huge abdominal mass lesion composed mainly of lipomatous tissues. All laboratory data were normal. What is the most likely diagnosis for this patient's condition?

A 23-year-old Korean woman presented with asymptomatic dark brown macules on her left leg for 2 years. Initially, one or two dark brown macules appeared and gradually spread without any preceding erythematous or scaly skin eruption. She reported no history of prolonged sun exposure or trauma at the lesion site. Upon examination, linear streaks of dark brown macules were observed from the left ankle, across the calf, to the thigh, following Blaschko's lines. There was no oral or nail involvement. Skin biopsy showed atrophic epidermis, basal hydropic degeneration with sparse perivascular lymphohistiocytic infiltrates, and numerous melanophages. What is the most likely diagnosis for this patient?

A 1-month-old girl was referred to the genetics clinic for evaluation of testicle-like masses observed during herniorrhaphy. She had bilateral inguinal hernias noted just after birth and laparoscopy showed no uterus and testicle-like masses near the bilateral inguinal canals. Born at a gestational age of 38 weeks with normal postnatal development, she had a normal female external genitalia with a blind short vaginal pouch and no Müllerian duct derivatives on genitography. Sonography revealed testes in the right lower quadrant of the abdomen and left inguinal canal. Her karyotype was 46,XY, and genetic analysis identified a hemizygous AR gene mutation. What is the most likely diagnosis?

A 59-year-old man with chronic kidney failure was referred for a GBCA MRI due to severe claudication. He received 17.5 ml of gadobutrol. One month prior, his creatinine was 190 μM with an MDRD GFR of 34 ml/min, indicating CKD Stage 3. Within a week after the MRI, he developed a universal rash examined by a dermatologist, revealing an increased number of CD34-positive spindle cells arranged in a 'tram-tracking' pattern, characteristic of a specific condition. He later experienced muscle and joint pain, along with symmetrical thickening and hardening of the skin on the lateral parts of the femur. Histological examination showed dermal and subcutaneous fibrosis with a sparse subepidermal mucinosis. Negative autoantibodies ruled out other fibrotic conditions. What is the likely diagnosis?

A 63-year-old female presented with a 2-day history of palpitations, shortness of breath, and chest pain, along with chest heaviness during deep inspiration both at rest and during ambulation. Her past medical history includes hypertension controlled with medications, and she denies smoking. An EKG indicated supraventricular tachycardia with a heart rate of 170 beats per minute. Blood pressure was 123/83 mm Hg, and her oxygen saturation was 97% on room air. Physical examination showed mild distress, normal heart sounds, no jugular venous distention, and clear lungs on auscultation. Despite treatments with adenosine and metoprolol, her arrhythmia persisted, leading to the administration of amiodarone. A chest X-ray showed pulmonary vascular congestion with cardiomegaly. Following admission, her blood pressure dropped to 97/65 mm Hg, and oxygen requirements increased, necessitating 2 L of oxygen via nasal cannula. A CT angiogram revealed multiple pulmonary emboli bilaterally and a large pericardial effusion, along with a 7mm nodule in the right upper lobe and mediastinal adenopathy. Echocardiogram showed ejection fraction of 60-65%, apical diastolic collapse, and large pericardial effusion. What is the likely diagnosis?

A 71-year-old man with a history of hypertrophic cardiomyopathy and moderate mitral regurgitation presents with a 3-week history of fever, general malaise, dyspnea, and chest pain following a dental extraction 2 months prior. On examination, he is in severe respiratory distress and has a pansystolic murmur. Laboratory findings show elevated cardiac biomarkers: high-sensitivity cardiac troponin T at 4266 µg/L, creatine kinase at 1705 U/L, and elevated acute phase reactants including leukocytosis with neutrophilia, high erythrocyte sedimentation rate, elevated C-reactive protein, and procalcitonin. Transthoracic echocardiography reveals a left ventricular ejection fraction of 20%, hypokinesis of certain heart segments, and a large eccentric jet of mitral regurgitation. Transoesophageal echocardiography shows severe mitral regurgitation and an oscillating mobile vegetation. Coronary angiogram indicates thrombus causing occlusion of the coronary artery. What is the most likely diagnosis?

A 45-year-old female with a history of HIV on antiretroviral therapy presents with multiple skin-colored, firm nodules on the left thigh, previously treated as cutaneous tuberculosis, but the lesions increased in size and number over 8 months. Histopathological examination shows diffuse infiltration of the dermis and subcutaneous tissue by large round lymphoid cells with centroblastic morphology, with no evidence of epidermotropism, and a clear grenz zone separating neoplastic cells from the epidermis. Immunohistochemistry reveals neoplastic cells positive for leukocyte common antigen, CD20, CD19, and CD79a, with a Mib-1 labeling index of 80%-90%. Large lymphoid cells are negative for bcl-2, MUM-1, CD10 and positive for bcl-6. What is the likely diagnosis?

A 11-day-old girl, born from a third-degree consanguineous marriage with a birth weight of 2.8 kg, presented with lethargy and refusal to feed since day 5 of life. Upon examination, she showed signs of shock and experienced a cardiac arrest, which was revived after resuscitation. The infant was severely dehydrated with no signs of virilization. Laboratory tests revealed metabolic acidosis, hyponatremia, and hyperkalemia, along with electrocardiographic changes. Despite treatment attempts with fludrocortisone, calcium gluconate, insulin infusion, K-binding resin, and sodium bicarbonate infusion, her hyperkalemia remained elevated, ranging between 9 and 11 mEq/L. She experienced significant weight loss and persistent dyselectrolytemia, necessitating increased doses of fludrocortisone and sodium chloride supplementation. Given these clinical findings and treatment resistance, what could be the underlying diagnosis?

A 48-year-old white female presents with yellowish asymptomatic micropapules that first appeared in the cervical region five years ago and later progressed to the axillae and cubital fossae. She has a history of arterial hypertension but denies any family history of similar skin conditions. Dermatological examination reveals coalescent yellowish papules forming plaques distributed symmetrically in the cervical region, axillas, and cubital fossae. Cardiological evaluation shows a normal electrocardiogram and echocardiogram. Right ophthalmoscopy identifies angioid streaks, confirmed by retinography and angiography. What is the likely diagnosis?

A 5-year-old female patient presents with swelling and pain in the right mandibular region. Initial antibiotic treatment provided temporary relief, but her symptoms recurred. Computed tomography (CT) shows an osteolytic, well-defined, buccolingual, expansile lesion in the mandible, coupled with a profuse periosteal reaction. Laboratory tests, including a complete blood count and other parameters, showed no notable systemic symptoms. An incisional biopsy was performed. What is the likely diagnosis for this mandibular condition?

A 65-year-old retired teacher with no family history of mental illness presented with a one and a half year history of mental illness following psychosocial stressors. Initial symptoms included sadness of mood, poor socialization, anhedonia, marked anxiety, decreased sleep and appetite, and ideas of worthlessness and hopelessness. He developed delusions of catastrophe, nihilism, poverty, and persecution, believing his organs stopped functioning and that he was dead. His condition led to self-starvation and multiple suicide attempts. Medical examination revealed hypertension, malnutrition, nutritional large fiber neuropathy, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, and chronic otitis media, but no abnormalities in thyroid function or MRI brain. What neuropsychiatric condition could explain his symptoms, including delusions of non-existence and self-starvation?

A 13-year-old boy was admitted to the emergency room with acute, severe abdominal pain, nausea, vomiting, and 6 to 7 episodes of fresh bloody diarrhea within two hours. The toilet bowl was filled with bright red, turbid water due to a relatively large amount of bloody diarrhea. He had been taking amoxicillin-clavulanate and nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs for three days for acute otitis media, as prescribed by a local clinic. His vital signs were within normal limits for his age, but physical examination showed abdominal tenderness in the periumbilical area. Laboratory tests revealed white blood cells at 17,300/µL with 79% neutrophils, hemoglobin at 14.8 g/dL, platelets at 288,000/µL, and C-reactive protein at 0.34 g/dL. Other chemistry tests and coagulation profiles were normal. Abdominal CT revealed colitis with edematous wall thickening from the ascending colon to the splenic flexure. Colonoscopy showed severe mucosal hemorrhage, erythema, and granular erosions particularly severe in the hepatic flexure area, but stool PCR tests for common enteric pathogens were negative. Considering these findings, what diagnosis should be considered?

A 42-year-old Thai woman presented with sub-acute dizziness and an unsteady gait. Two weeks later, she developed memory impairment and deterioration of concentration. Her interest and pleasure in all activities, as well as her speech, diminished remarkably. Her condition became progressively worse, and eventually she became akinetic-rigid and mute. Later, spontaneous myoclonic jerks were present in her distal limbs. Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) showed high signal intensity in the bilateral caudate nucleus, putamen and left frontotemporal cortex on T2-weighted and diffusion-weighted imaging (DWI). Electroencephalography (EEG) revealed generalized and synchronous periodic sharp wave complexes occurring at intervals of 0.6–0.8 seconds. What is the most likely diagnosis for this patient based on her clinical history and examination findings?

A 44-year-old male presents with dyspnea on exertion and cough persisting for several months, despite treatment with broad-spectrum antibiotics and anti-tubercular drugs. Radiological evaluation shows bilateral lung nodules with mediastinal lymphadenopathy, bilateral pneumonia, and a right-sided pleural effusion. CT of the abdomen reveals large kidneys with tumefactive hypodense lesions, hepatosplenomegaly, and retroperitoneal lymphadenopathy. Laboratory tests show an elevated erythrocyte sedimentation rate, normal angiotensin converting enzyme levels, and significantly elevated gamma globulin fraction without an "M" spike. Kidney biopsy shows glomeruli surrounded by dense sclerotic interstitium with lymphoplasmacytoid infiltrates and numerous eosinophils; immunohistochemistry is positive for CD138 and reveals IgG4 positive plasma cells >40/hpf. A 12-year-old girl presents with a persistent skin rash on her left ear lasting over 4 weeks, accompanied by dyspnea, sore throat, and low-grade fever.
